content:
"Instead of disposing of the woody offcuts from your winter garden tidy-up by burning them or feeding them into a shredder, consider turning them into a “dead hedge”. Built from prunings and branches, it can form an effective barrier against gusty weather, provide shelter and nesting spaces for insects, birds and other small creatures, and create a natural-looking boundary between different parts of your garden. To make one, drive in sturdy stakes or reclaimed fence posts in two parallel lines about 50cm apart, then weave and pack your cut material between them, starting with the thickest pieces along the bottom. Keep topping it up as you generate more prunings, and expect the structure to compress and sink a little as it settles.

If your festive haul was disappointing, you could lift your spirits by reserving a copy of The Book Of Seeds by Paul Smith, formerly of Kew’s Millennium Seed Bank. Due out in February, it’s an opulent showcase of 600 striking and unusual seeds, ranging from quirky, hairlike forms to dust-fine orchid seeds.

For winter interest in the garden, try a winter-blooming clematis in a warm, sunny, protected position, where it can flower from December through February with scented, creamy bells in various forms and sizes. Is there anything else I can help with?"
